extracted.intended_audience: editors and writers (copyeditors, journalists, publishers, authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for when to capitalize names, terms, titles, and related language categories in running text, following Chicago Manual of Style conventions. Covers organizations, historical and cultural terms, religious language, military terminology, awards, calendar items, and more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of official organizations and parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Official names of national and international organizations, alliances, political movements, and parties are capitalized; words like party, union, and movement are capitalized when part of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “the Labor Party in Israel”; the African National Congress (ANC); Arab Socialist Ba‘th Party. When 'party' is not part of the official name (the African National Congress party), treat generics accordingly. Terms identifying formal members or adherents are usually capitalized (e.g., 'a Socialist', 'a Republican').

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems of thought vs. adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of systems of thought and references to adherents are often lowercased, though a work may choose consistent capitalization for philosophy, organization, and adherents to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'an eighteenth-century precursor of socialism'; 'a communist at heart' (lowercase). But in a work about communism one may capitalize both 'Communism' and 'Communist' consistently to avoid editorial headaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonliteral or metaphorical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonliteral or metaphorical uses of political or ideological terms are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'fascist parenting techniques'; 'nazi tendencies' (lowercase in metaphorical senses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherents of unofficial political groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Names for adherents of political groups or movements that are not formal parties are usually lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'anarchist(s)', 'centrist(s)', 'independent(s)', 'moderate(s)', 'mugwump(s)'. Exceptions: 'the Opposition' (British/Canadian usage) and capitalized usages for 'the Left'/'the Right' or 'Tea Party' (modeled on established parties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of institutions and companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Full names of institutions, groups, companies, and the names of their departments are capitalized; generic terms are usually lowercased when used alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the University of Chicago; the university'; 'the Department of History; the department'; 'the Board of Trustees of the University of Chicago; the board of trustees; the board.' Generic terms like 'company' or 'university' are lowercased when used alone (unless in promotional materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of corporate names with unusual styling
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate logotype or stylized lowercase/uppercase names can generally be rendered in regular capitalization in running text; internal capitals and mixed-case forms are usually preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult corporate 'About' or copyright statements for preferred usage. Examples: 'Intel (not intel)', 'Adidas (not adidas)', 'eBay' is acceptable. If company insists on all lowercase and style permits, an initial capital may be applied as editorial expediency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of associations, societies, unions, meetings, conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Full names of associations, societies, unions, meetings, and conferences, and often their shortened forms, are capitalized; generic terms used alone are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Congress of Industrial Organizations; CIO; the union'; 'Girl Scouts of the United States of America; a Girl Scout; a Scout.' A substantive title given to a single meeting or conference is enclosed in quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclosing titles of single meetings in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantive title given to a single meeting, conference, speech, or discussion is enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '“Inside the Mind of a Master Procrastinator,” a TED talk by Tim Urban posted in March 2016.' For lecture series see separate guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical designations for historical periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical designations for periods are usually lowercased, though some may be treated as proper nouns (both numeral and term capitalized) to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the twenty-first century' (lowercase); 'the second millennium BCE' (uppercase BCE). Usage notes reference numeral rules in other sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive designations for historical periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive designations of periods are usually lowercased, except for proper names or to avoid ambiguity with a generic term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ancient Greece', 'the antebellum period', 'the Romantic period' (traditionally capitalized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional period names capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain traditional period names are capitalized by convention or to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Enlightenment', 'the Renaissance', 'the Dark Ages', 'the Gilded Age', 'the Progressive Era'. See list in text for commonly capitalized traditional names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of prehistoric and geological period names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of prehistoric cultural periods and geological periods are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Bronze Age', 'the Iron Age', 'the Ice Age', 'the Stone Age'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern-period style names often lowercased
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar modern descriptors (e.g., 'information age') are often lowercased unless context or convention dictates capitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the information age', 'the nuclear age' (lowercase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical events and programs capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of many major historical events and programs are conventionally capitalized; more recent or generically-described events often are lowercased, and when in doubt opt for lowercase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples capitalized: 'the Great Depression', 'the Industrial Revolution', 'the New Deal', 'Prohibition'. Examples often lowercased: 'the baby boom', 'the crash of 1929', 'the war on terror' (lowercase generic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speeches: capitalization of notable speech titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of a select few famous speeches are traditionally capitalized; many others are usually lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples capitalized: 'Washington’s Farewell Address', 'the Gettysburg Address', 'Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech'; other inaugural or occasional addresses may be lowercased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named storms and meteorological phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Named hurricanes and tropical cyclones and many other named meteorological phenomena are capitalized; natural phenomena identified generically by a place-name or year are usually lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Hurricane Katrina' (capitalized); 'the 2005 hurricane' (lowercased). Use the pronoun 'it' rather than 'he' or 'she' when referring to named storms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major sporting events capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Full names of major sporting events are capitalized; generic references are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Kentucky Derby; the NBA Finals; the Olympic Games; the World Cup; the finals (generic)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural movements and styles capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Nouns and adjectives designating cultural styles, movements, and schools are capitalized if derived from proper nouns; words like 'school' and 'movement' remain lowercased; some movements may be capitalized to distinguish them from generic words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Beat movement; the Beats', 'Impressionism' (capitalized when treated as a proper name), 'impressionism' may be lowercased in general prose. If you capitalize one movement consistently, do so across the work to avoid uneven capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of acts, treaties, and government programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal or accepted titles of acts, treaties, pacts, plans, policies, and programs are capitalized; incomplete or generic forms are usually lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Bill of Rights', 'the Constitution of the United States', 'the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993; FMLA; the 1993 act', 'food stamps' (generic lowercased). For legal citation see other sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic references to pending legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal or purely descriptive references to pending legislation are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The anti-injunction bill was introduced on Tuesday.' (lowercase 'bill' in generic reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal case names formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of legal cases are italicized when mentioned in running text; the abbreviation 'v.' may appear in roman but Chicago recommends italics. In footnotes or legal dictionaries roman is sometimes used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Bloomfield Village Drain Dist. v. Keefe' italicized in running text. In discussion case names may be shortened: 'the Miranda case' or simply 'Miranda.' See legal citation sections for detailed rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of awards and prizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of awards and prizes are capitalized; some generic terms used with the names may be lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; a Nobel Prize winner; a Nobel Prize–winning physiologist'; 'a Pulitzer in journalism' (generic 'Pulitzer' usage may vary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths and pledges capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal oaths and pledges are usually lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the oath of citizenship', 'marriage vows', 'the Hippocratic oath' (lowercased), but institutional or specific named pledges like 'the Pledge of Allegiance' are capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic subjects capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic subjects are not capitalized unless they form part of a department name, an official course name, or are proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'history of religions' (lowercase); 'Jones is chair of the Committee on Comparative Literature' (chair title/department capitalized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courses of study capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Official course names and course numbers are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I am signing up for Archaeology 101'; 'Basic Manuscript Editing' (official course titles capitalized). Generic descriptions of classes are lowercased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture series and individual lecture titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of lecture series are capitalized; titles for individual lectures are capitalized and usually enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'This year’s Robinson Memorial Lectures'; 'The first lecture, “How Nightingale Got Her Way,” was a sellout.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Calendar: days, months, and seasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of days and months are capitalized; the four seasons are lowercased (except when used to denote a journal issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Tuesday', 'November' (capitalized); 'spring', 'fall' (lowercased), except 'Fall 2020 issue' as a journal designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holidays capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of secular and religious holidays and officially designated days or seasons are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Christmas Day', 'Mother’s Day', 'Election Day', 'Ramadan', 'Hanukkah', 'Kwanzaa'. Some observances like 'a bank holiday' are lowercased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and time zones formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: When spelled out, designations of time zones are lowercased; their abbreviations are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'eastern standard time; EST', 'Pacific daylight time; PDT', 'daylight saving time; DST'. See other sections for numerals/time formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of deities and revered persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of deities and revered persons are capitalized; alternative or descriptive names for God are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'God, Allah, Jehovah, the Holy Ghost or the Holy Spirit, the Lord, Providence.' Respect conventions like 'G‑d' where preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns referring to religious figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns referring to God or Jesus are not capitalized unless a particular author or publisher prefers otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'They prayed to God that he would deliver them.' Note that many Bible translations use lowercase pronouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of major religions and adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of major religions, their adherents, and adjectives derived from them are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Buddhism; Buddhist', 'Christianity; Christian', 'Islam; Islamic; Muslim', 'Judaism; Jew; Jewish'. Generic or nonreligious terms like 'atheism' and 'agnosticism' are lowercased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominations, sects, orders capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of denominations, communions, sects, orders, and religious movements are capitalized; adjectives and adherents are capitalized as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Amish; Anglicanism; the Episcopal Church; Jesuit(s); Hasidism; Reform Judaism.' Some terms may be lowercased in nonsectarian contexts (e.g., 'Puritanism' lowercased when used generically).

rubrics_metrics.name: “Church” as institution vs. part of proper name
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to the institution of religion, 'church' is usually lowercased; 'Church' is capitalized when part of a formal name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'church and state', 'the early church'; but 'the United Methodist Church' (formal name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic versus specific religious terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Many terms that are lowercased when used generically may be capitalized when they are the name of a specific religion, sect, or movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'spiritualist' (lowercase generic) vs. 'Spiritualist' if it denotes a named movement or group in context. Use dictionaries when unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious jurisdictions capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of official divisions within organized religions (dioceses, synods, archdioceses) are capitalized; generic terms alone are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Archdiocese of Chicago; the archdiocese', 'the Holy See' (capitalized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Places of worship names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of buildings in which religious congregations meet are capitalized; the generic terms used alone are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Bethany Evangelical Lutheran Church; the church', 'Temple Emanuel; the temple; the synagogue', 'Babri Mosque; the mosque.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Councils and synods capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepted names of historic councils and the official names of modern counterparts are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Council of Chalcedon', 'the Second Vatican Council; Vatican II', 'the Synod of Whitby.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptures and highly revered works capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of scriptures and other highly revered religious works are capitalized but not usually italicized (unless used as a published-work title).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Bible (but biblical)', 'the Bhagavad Gita', 'the Koran or Qur’an (Qur’anic)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other bible versions and names
rubrics_metrics.description: Other names and versions of the Hebrew and Christian bibles are usually capitalized but not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Authorized Version or the King James Version', 'the New Revised Standard Version', 'the Douay (or Rheims-Douay) Version.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Books and sections of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of the books of the Bible and named sections are capitalized but not italicized; the word 'book' is usually lowercased and 'gospel' and 'epistle' are usually capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Genesis; Job; 2 Chronicles; Psalms (but a psalm)', 'the Hebrew scriptures or the Old Testament', 'the Epistles; the Gospels.' In works using many biblical terms, choose consistent treatment (all lowercased or capitalized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Named prayers, creeds, canticles
rubrics_metrics.description: Named prayers, canticles, creeds, and similar items are usually capitalized; parables and miracles are usually lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Lord’s Prayer; the Nicene Creed; Kaddish; the Sermon on the Mount' (capitalized), but 'the parable of the prodigal son' (lowercase 'parable').

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious events, concepts, services, and objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious events and concepts of major theological importance are often capitalized; used generically they are lowercased. Doctrines and common principles are usually lowercased. Names of services and rites are usually lowercased, with some traditional exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples capitalized: 'the Crucifixion; the Exodus; the Second Coming' (theologically important events). Generic: 'crucifixion was a common form of execution.' Services: 'baptism; bar mitzvah; confirmation' (lowercase). Eucharistic terms like 'the Eucharist' and 'Holy Communion' are traditionally capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of religious use
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects of religious use or significance are usually lowercased, especially in nonreligious contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'altar; mandala; sacred pipe; ark; mezuzah; sanctuary; chalice and paten; rosary; stations of the cross' (lowercase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of military forces and troop units
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of armies, navies, air forces, fleets, regiments, battalions, companies, corps, and similar units are capitalized; generic uses of 'army' and 'navy' are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Army of Northern Virginia; the Army; Royal Navy; RAF; the Mounties; the Mountie.' Unofficial well-known names (e.g., 'Green Berets') are capitalized. Generic plurals or collective references often remain lowercased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wars, revolutions, battles, and campaigns capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of major wars and revolutions are capitalized; generic or more recent/unresolved conflicts are often lowercased. Famous battles and campaigns often are capitalized; for others consult an encyclopedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples capitalized: 'American Civil War; World War II; Korean War; Battle of Britain; Battle of Bunker Hill; the Blitz.' Examples often lowercased: 'the civil war in South Sudan; the Ukrainian unrest.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Military awards capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific names of military medals and awards are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Medal of Honor; Purple Heart; Victoria Cross; Distinguished Flying Cross.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of ships and vessels formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of specific ships and other vessels are both capitalized and italicized; abbreviations like USS or HMS are not italicized and, when used, the generic ship word should not be repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'USS Enterprise (CVN-65) was...' (include hull numbers where necessary to avoid confusion). 'HMS Frolic; the British ship Frolic.' When abbreviations precede a name, do not write 'the ship' plus the abbreviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other vehicle and program names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of makes and classes of aircraft, models of automobiles, names of trains or train runs, and names of space programs are capitalized but not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Acela Express; Concorde; Project Apollo; Boeing 787 Dreamliner; Subaru Forester.' Spacecraft names may be exceptions (some are italicized as vessel names).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns for vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: When a pronoun is used to refer to a vessel, prefer the neuter 'it' or 'its' rather than 'she' or 'her'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The ship moved slowly; it entered the harbor.'
